analysis.one_liner: Lets patients appeal managed-care denials to outside reviewers and sue health plans for negligent coverage decisions.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the patient protections 59-36 in June 2001, but the House held the bill at the desk for two years without ever scheduling a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill set rules for HMOs and other managed-care plans: claims denials would have to be decided on medical timelines, patients would get the right to an internal appeal and then an independent outside review, and plans would have to cover emergency care without prior approval, let patients see specialists and OB-GYNs directly, cover breast-cancer hospital stays as long as the doctor says is needed, and cover participation in approved clinical trials. It also created a federal right to sue a plan for injury or death caused by a negligent coverage decision, though the Senate-passed version barred punitive damages and let employers off the hook unless they directly took part in the decision. No patient in America had these rights as federal law.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans enrolled in employer health plans, HMOs, and individual insurance policies — essentially everyone with private coverage. The bill guaranteed binding outside review of medical denials, faster decisions for urgent care (72 hours), direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, emergency care without prior approval, and the right to recover damages when a plan's negligent decision causes injury or death.

how_it_helps.text: Every denied claim involving medical judgment — medical necessity, experimental treatment — would go to an independent external review, whose decision is binding on the plan, at no cost to patients who are indigent and with the fee refunded if the denial is reversed [S4].
Plans must decide prior-authorization requests within 14 days (72 hours when a doctor certifies delay would jeopardize life or health), and treat missed deadlines as denials eligible for appeal [S4].

Patients get direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, emergency services without prior authorization, timely access to specialists, and breast-cancer hospital stays for as long as the attending physician determines medically necessary [S3].
Plans cannot use physician incentive arrangements that reward limiting care, cannot gag doctors from advising patients about treatment options, and must pay claims promptly [S3].
Plans and issuers become liable for economic and noneconomic damages if they fail to exercise ordinary care in a denial and that failure proximately causes personal injury or death [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employer plans they administer would bear the cost of new utilization-review programs, fast-track decision timelines, independent external reviews (the plan pays the reviewer's cost), and legal liability for negligent denials; some of that cost would likely pass through to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued that expanded liability would raise premiums and lead employers to drop coverage; the bill itself contained that safeguard — an annual Institute of Medicine study and automatic repeal of the federal lawsuit provisions if more than one million people lost coverage as a result [S3].
The Senate-passed version was narrower than a full right to sue: damages were available only for decisions not eligible for independent medical review, and punitive damages were excluded [S3].
Plans pay the cost of external reviews, and patients could face filing fees up to $25 (waived for the indigent and refunded if the denial is reversed) [S4].
The new timelines and documentation rules add administrative work for plans and the doctors and hospitals that deal with them, particularly for small self-insured employers [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gave patients something they otherwise could not get: an outside, binding check on an HMO's decision to deny care, plus a legal remedy when negligence costs a life. The main cost is borne by insurers and self-insured employers, with possible premium pass-through, and the bill's own trigger — automatic repeal of the lawsuit provisions if coverage losses exceeded one million people — was designed to cap that risk. The genuine design compromise is that liability applies only to non-medical (contractual) denials and bars punitive damages, which is weaker than advocates originally wanted but stronger than the near-total immunity patients had under ERISA at the time.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 59-36 on June 29, 2001, but House Republican leaders never scheduled a vote; the bill sat at the House desk until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The Senate agreed to a motion to proceed to the bill 98-0 on June 21, 2001, with every Democrat and 47 of 49 Republicans voting yes [S7].
Republican senators twice tried to send the bill back to committees — a Frist motion rejected 39-61 on June 26, with 37 of 49 Republicans in favor and all but 2 Democrats opposed [S8].
The Senate passed the bill 59-36 on June 29, 2001: all 50 Democrats voted yes, 9 of 49 Republicans joined them, and the lone Independent voted no [S10].

The House received the Senate-passed bill on November 19, 2002, and held it at the desk — meaning it was never referred or scheduled for a vote — and it expired with the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed-care companies came out ahead: they never had to accept binding outside review of medical denials or face liability for negligent coverage decisions. House leaders who controlled the floor calendar also avoided a vote on a bill that had already passed the Senate with bipartisan support.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bipartisan Patient Protection Act in June 2001 and led it to Senate passage.

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Lead Democratic cosponsor of the bill, part of the McCain-Kennedy-Edwards trio that drove the patients' bill of rights.

for.name: John Edwards
for.what_they_did: Original Democratic cosponsor of the bill, part of the McCain-Kennedy-Edwards trio.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the Senate floor weeks after Democrats took Senate control; the motion to proceed passed 98-0.

for.name: 50 of 50 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for final passage; also voted unanimously to block a motion to recommit the bill to committees.

against.name: 35 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage of the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and leaders who control the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate-passed bill on November 19, 2002, and held it at the desk; the House never voted on it.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to send the bill to three committees, which failed 39-61.

against.name: Gordon Smith
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to commit the bill to the Finance Committee, which the Senate ruled out of order on a 57-41 vote.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Senate patients' bill of rights and threatened a veto, backing a narrower House alternative instead.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats were unanimous for the bill (50-0 on final passage), and 9 of 49 Republicans crossed over to pass it 59-36; 35 of 49 Republicans voted no, and Republican senators offered the motions to recommit that failed along near-party lines.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: The bill strips their near-total immunity under ERISA: denials based on medical judgment become subject to binding independent review, decision timelines are enforced with penalties, and the plan is liable for injury or death caused by negligent coverage decisions. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against patients who wanted their denials checked.

Employers are shielded from lawsuit liability unless they directly participate in a denied claim decision, but they must comply with the appeals and access requirements and feared rising coverage costs. Business groups fought the bill largely over this liability question.

industries.industry: Doctors and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bans incentive arrangements that reward doctors for denying care, protects doctor-patient communication about treatment options, requires prompt payment of claims, and protects providers from retaliation for patient advocacy.

The bill requires every medically reviewable denial to go to an independent external reviewer whose costs the plan pays, creating a certified industry of outside reviewers. Patients gain from this channel rather than losing to it.
